# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–30 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Spring of eighth year after Waterloo, continuing through summer into winter. Year is 1830 (French Revolution year). Now mid-April.
- **Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens," near Queen's Crawley); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Beccles; Quenwick; Harrowgate; Dunwick; Liverpool; San Francisco; California; Salt Lake City; New Mexico; Arizona; Mexico; Vera Cruz; Queenstown.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix). All other property valueless shares.
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc (Chapters 27–30)
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance—hiding degradation evidence, offering tender looks, falsely claiming virtuous past. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Within week, Jos became her "entirely slave." Changed habits; praised Dobbin constantly to Emmy; claimed she behaved cruelly toward him. Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner with adjacent suite, carriage, entertainments.

**Insurance and Death**: Jos effected heavy insurance. Dobbin procured prolonged leave, alarmed. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged payment; Rebecca dared them to refuse, declared herself victim of "infamous conspiracy." Solicitors Messrs. Burke, Thurtell, and Hayes triumphed; £2,000 paid. **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication with Rebecca.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declined to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham, where strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in works of piety, church attendance, appears on all Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin's Resolution (Chapter 29)
**Becky's Revelation**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy." Produced letter: George "wanted me to run away with him—gave it me under your nose, the day before he was shot." **"Dobbin forced him to keep his word."**

**Amelia's Transformation**: Emmy wept; internal struggle: "Was she most grieved because the idol of her life was tumbled down...or glad because the barrier was removed which modesty had placed between her and a new, a real affection? 'There is nothing to forbid me now,' she thought. 'I may love him with all my heart now.'"

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present at ceremony. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to Mrs. Dobbin's child; they became great friends.

## Lady Carbury and Family (Chapter 30)
**Lady Carbury**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. **"The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was."** Devoted to children, especially Felix. Back drawing-room (divided by permanently closed doors) is workspace for writing books and contriving systems to inveigle editors and critics.

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him as boy and man; almost proud of his vices. Philosophy: "carpe diem." Possesses two unpaid-for horses. Demands money from mother to maintain appearance in Grosvenor Square. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming (still retains winnings). **Currently considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress); at Melmotte ball, waltzes with Marie, studying words as lesson ("I do") to convince poor girl he could love her.** Left ball early to Beargarden—gambling devil hot within him. **Since Roger's offer to Henrietta, Felix has "gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment."** Despite debts, claims to be "all right"; boasts money in pocket. Roger suspects talk of giving home for Henrietta is delusional. Felix lacks courage to shake off Roger violently and dreads Roger's words with "craven fear." **Now a director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company.**

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance commenced. Cousin Roger Carbury (of Carbury Hall, nearly forty) passionately in love with her. Paul Montague is another gentleman whom Henrietta has seen. Roger offered hand in marriage with declaration: "Very serious to me." **Paul Montague fell into love with Henrietta during second visit to Carbury Hall.** Scene between Roger and Paul lasted above an hour with very hot words. Paul packed clothes and was driven by Roger to railway station without seeing either lady, departing in tears. Roger blessed him at platform. **Henrietta rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young to marry and age disparity insurmountable; admitted "even that disparity was not now her strongest reason for feeling sure that she could not marry Roger Carbury."** Within week, Paul Montague returned "as a still dear friend," having promised not to see Henrietta again for three months but nothing further. Paul believed he could yield if Roger could make anything of his offer. Though Paul doubted his finances (share in "doubtful business of Fisker, Montague, and Montague, in a wretched little town 250 miles further off than San Francisco"), he declared he had money and would not give up Henrietta on account of finances. Roger would not accede to justice of Paul's argument.

**Lady Carbury's Divided Concerns**: Solicitude for son greatly increases desire for daughter's union with Roger. Roger came to London horrified that man with no income has hunters. Roger recommended Lady Carbury give up house in town, find home for daughter elsewhere, let Felix "bear the brunt of his own misdoings." **Roger believes remedy lies in mother's conduct: were she not foolishly weak, she would divide utterly from son and leave him to suffer utter penury.** Roger fired last shot: "You will ruin your sister, and break your mother's heart." Roger resolved to warn Henrietta against Melmotte connection and advised her to regard him as elder brother. **Roger remains firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds to old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile."**

## The Melmottes (Chapter 30)
**Augustus Melmotte, Esq.**: Arrived in London from Paris within last two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks native language fluently with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair, expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face; repellent unless attracted by internal consideration. Magnificent in expenditure, powerful in doings, successful in business. **Miles Grendall serves as his usher/secretary in his office.** **Now chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company with two million dollars of shares allocated to himself.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Said to have been Bohemian Jewess; speaks very little English.

**Marie Melmotte**: Spoke as Mademoiselle Marie; now speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough** (bankrupt, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered). Had experience with Lord Nidderdale, who half-laughingly said he "might just as well take her for his wife." **People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man.**

## Roger Carbury of Carbury Hall (Chapter 30)
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father before him likewise. Carbury parish named for family. **Carbury Chase (partly in Carbury parish, partly Bundlesham) belongs unfortunately in entirety to Bundlesham estate.**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme (Chapter 30)
**The Enterprise**: Grand proposal for railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through fertile lands of New Mexico and Arizona into Mexican Republic, running by city of Mexico, terminating at Gulf port of Vera Cruz. **Distance approximately 2,000 miles; no computation made as to probable cost.** Fisker considers such questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government through territories; correspondence maintained with President of Mexican Republic.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock to be taken "at par"; shares to be sold at premium. Goal to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum.

**Key Players**:
- **Hamilton K. Fisker**: American, approximately forty. Partner in firm Fisker, Montague, and Montague (San Francisco). Small, shining man with well-twisted moustache, greasy brown hair becoming bald at top. Gorgeously dressed with silk waistcoat, chains, carries little stick. Troubled by no shyness, scruples, or fears. Supremely confident, good-humoured, audacious, clever. Previously engaged in California financing.

- **Paul Montague**: Junior member of Fisker, Montague, and Montague. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but finds himself unable to resist the man's combination of good humour, audacity, and cleverness. Trembles for his money and wishes never to see Fisker again. Obeyed Fisker's telegram order (sent at Queenstown from New York liner) to meet at Liverpool immediately. Met Fisker at great railway hotel at Liverpool; Fisker displayed maps, schedules, printed programmes. Fisker convinced Paul to write letter inviting Melmotte to meet him. **Letter dated from Langham Hotel, posted at Euston Square Railway Station upon Fisker's arrival.** **Following morning, Paul and Fisker travelled to London together.** Fisker presented himself in Abchurch Lane office; letter resulted in twenty-minute wait before audience with Melmotte granted.

**Launch and Direction**: **At end of fortnight from Fisker's arrival in London, company fully launched in England with body of London directors, of whom Mr. Melmotte is chairman. Among directors: Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe, Esq. (Member of Parliament for Staines, Jewish persuasion), Lord Nidderdale (also in Parliament), and Mr. Paul Montague.** Fisker fully satisfied with progress. Paul Montague still troubled by doubts; Melmotte's reality as commercial fact makes refusal to believe in scheme impossible. Melmotte had telegraph at command, made close inquiries as though San Francisco and Salt Lake City were London suburbs. Though Melmotte tower of strength, many thought him "built upon the sands."

**Post-Launch Activities (Mid-April)**: **Paul took to living good deal at the Beargarden; reasoned man dines cheaper at club than elsewhere, though his dinners were not cheap.** Saw good deal of brother directors Sir Felix Carbury and Lord Nidderdale; entertained Lord Alfred once at club; dined twice with Melmotte amidst all magnificence of merchant-princely hospitality in Grosvenor Square. **Suggested by Fisker that Paul enter himself for great Marie Melmotte plate. Lord Nidderdale again declared intention of running due to pressure from interested tradesmen; became director of Mexican Railway Company. Sir Felix is favourite for race among fashionable circles generally.** **Fisker still in London mid-April, justified by millions of dollars at stake belonging perhaps to widows and orphans. Fisker "had a good time" in London; made free of Beargarden as honorary member, spent good deal of money.** Greatness of operations relieved Fisker and Montague from necessity of looking to small expenses; champagne consumption increased, results deleterious. **Montague found he could not wake up on London mornings with thoughts as satisfactory as those at old Manor House (Carbury Hall).**
